articles.title_orig: Trump proposing new tariffs on 14 partners including China and EU
articles.title_zh: Trump proposing new tariffs on 14 partners including China and EU
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. is preparing new tariffs on 14 economies , including China, the EU, Japan and India, following investigations into what the Trump administration says are excess manufacturing practices that disadvantage U.S. commerce.
The administration launched those and other trade investigations in March , weeks after the Supreme Court unraveled a major piece of President Donald Trump 's tariff-heavy economic policy by striking down his "liberation day" duties. Trump has since been accused by critics of his tariffs of trying to revive the canceled duties using other legal authorities.
The latest action targets foreign economies that create, sustain or contribute to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors that the U.S. finds unreasonable and burdensome or restrictive to its commerce, a senior U.S. official told reporters Tuesday evening.
The new tariffs are "targeted," not blanket rates, and will vary for each economy, and many will not exceed the rates established in previously reached trade deals, said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the forthcoming duties.
The rates, which mostly range from 15% to 20%, are "not really additive" and generally will not stack on top of existing duties, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" Wednesday morning.
"In effect, it'll look more like a top up," Greer said. "When it all nets out, it really will just top up a few percentage points."
An exception is China, which faces a 20% rate under the new tariff policy, "so it will go up some," Greer said. But at the same time, both countries are moving to remove tariffs on some of each other's goods in what Greer called "stability-generating activity through this action."
The senior U.S. official said Tuesday that the 20% rate will come on top of the so-called forced technology transfer-related tariffs of roughly 25%, which were implemented during Trump's first presidential term. U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods will therefore reach about 45%, give or take for different goods, the official said.
Average U.S. tariffs rates on Chinese goods stood at about 36.5% as of July, according to the Congressional Research Service .
Greer also said on CNBC that the new policy likely will not take effect for months.
"We've talked to our trading partners about this. They know what we're proposing," he said. "I think a lot of this is baked in, and I don't think any of these would actually take effect earlier than a couple months from now."
The administration says the tariffs target what it calls "overcapacity" — excess industrial production, often supported by government subsidies, that allows cheaper goods to flood global markets and undercut U.S. producers.
China has disputed the allegations. "The so-called 'overcapacity' does not really exist," China's foreign ministry said Wednesday before the official reports were released by the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, according to Reuters.
The overcapacity levies are being imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The Trump administration invoked the same statute to launch investigations into 60 economies over alleged forced-labor issues.
Those investigations, which also began in March, led to broad tariffs of 10% to 12.5% on goods from dozens of countries covering 99.4% of U.S. imports.
The Section 301 actions came weeks after the Supreme Court struck down the near-global tariffs that Trump had enacted under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.
Shortly after the court's ruling, Trump invoked Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 to impose a 10% global tariff. That tariff expired after 150 days, and was immediately replaced with the forced-labor-related duties.
An ongoing lawsuit accuses the Trump administration of citing forced-labor issues as a "pretext" in pursuit of reviving Trump's worldwide tariff regime.

articles.title_orig: Market sell-off eases up, but AI doubts, tariffs and inflation still weigh down stocks
articles.title_zh: Market sell-off eases up, but AI doubts, tariffs and inflation still weigh down stocks
articles.content_orig:
U.S. stocks broadly slumped Wednesday, led by companies linked to the AI boom.
The volatile day began with a sharp sell-off that briefly sent the influential Nasdaq 100 index into bear market territory, which occurs when an index falls by 20% or more from its most recent high. The S&P 500 was down by as much as 3.2% in early trading.
But sentiment among traders and investors improved slightly over the course of the day.
An early beneficiary of the renewed optimism was Anthropic, the AI giant that staged a record-setting IPO last week, only to see its stock battered for three straight trading sessions. Shortly after midday, Anthropic was finally trading back above its IPO price of $83 per share.
Meanwhile, the Nasdaq Composite was down roughly 1.5% and the S&P 500 was lower by only 0.5%. The Dow was flat in early afternoon trading and just barely back over a symbolic 50,000.
Even as markets pulled back from their lows, Nvidia remained among the biggest losers in key indexes.  After soaring by 31% on Monday on news that its recently-departed CEO Jensen Huang would return to the C-suite, the stock was still lower by about 7% Wednesday, its second straight down day.
The return of Huang, a de facto ambassador for the artificial intelligence industry, briefly reassured investors that big AI firms, and the trillions of dollars they borrow and lend, would continue to grow without interruption.
Stock markets Monday staged their biggest one-day rally since April 2025, as the Nasdaq 100 skyrocketed 6.8% and the S&P 500 surged 4.7%.
President Donald Trump pushed Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang over the weekend despite multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy. Before the president stepped in, the board had been unequivocal that it did not plan to reinstate Huang.
Trump said Monday that he “probably” decided to intervene in Nvidia’s internal leadership decision because he was concerned about a market sell-off in the week after Huang’s departure fueled partly by investor concerns about how the CEO’s resignation would impact the broader AI industry.
But ever since Monday’s rally, markets have struggled to maintain that upward momentum.
“The risk-off tone has returned over the last 24 hours, as Monday’s rebound in tech stocks lost momentum once again,” Deutsche Bank strategists said in a note early Wednesday.
Before Monday’s one-day rally, stocks had faced weeks of selling, which pushed the Nasdaq 100 into correction territory on Friday, which is defined as a 10% drop from its last high.
Shares of semiconductor stocks, as tracked by the Philadelphia semiconductor index, have plunged more than 40% since their last peak in June. Stocks of companies that make data center and computer memory products have plummeted 60% over the same period.
AI-related sentiment has also been damaged further by frontier developer Anthropic, whose shares have spiraled lower since its initial public offering last week.
Stocks Wednesday likely faced additional pressure due to the looming Thanksgiving holiday.
U.S. markets will be closed Thursday and open for only a half-day of trading Friday.
Investors are more likely to cut their large or risky trades before extended weekends, in order to avoid being trapped in positions while events unfold.
On top of cracks in the AI sector, “matters weren’t helped by the latest tariff headlines,” Deutsche Bank’s team wrote.
On Wednesday, t he Trump administration unveiled a new wave of tariffs on the United States’ top trading partners, such as the European Union, China, Japan and a dozen more.
“It is another reminder that while the legal justification for tariffs keeps changing, US protectionism is becoming increasingly difficult to unwind,” ING senior trade economist Inga Fechner wrote in a note Wednesday.
That drove stocks down further, with the prospect that more tariffs could cause renewed trade tensions, a renewed inflation spike and cause a flare-up with a policy that had largely started to subside in recent months.
Even before Wednesday’s formal announcement, a spokesperson for the Chinese Commerce Ministry blasted the new import duties. “Tariff wars and trade wars are in the interests of neither side,” the spokesperson said. The ministry called it “political manipulation.”
“Some investors might have been caught off guard by news that the Administration is on track to release more tariffs, but the key question about the Administration unveiling new tariffs from the Section 301 overcapacity investigation has never been an issue of whether but when,” wrote Sarah Bianchi, chief strategist of international political affairs at Evercore ISI.
Compounding the negative pressure facing investors Wednesday, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge moved further away from its 2% goal.
The personal consumption expenditures index was 3.8% for October, up from 3.6% in September. Even excluding food and energy, the “core” inflation reading rose to 3.3%. It had been 3.1% the previous month.
The rise in core inflation readings is particularly noteworthy because it can indicate that higher gas prices sparked by the Iran war are spilling over into the rest of the economy.
It also raises the likelihood that the Fed will raise interest rates at its next meeting, which concludes with a rate decision Dec. 9.
Last week, a top Fed policymaker said the central bank needed to “shock people” with a larger rate hike than is typical.
“I’m very, very concerned about inflation,” Fed governor Christopher Waller said in a CNBC interview . “It’s kind of headed in the wrong direction, and it’s spreading out.”
Waller said the Fed needed to take “more aggressive actions,” such as hiking by 0.50%, more than the Fed’s usual 0.25% rate increase. “You might need to, like, shock people,” he said.
A rate hike would carry its own complications, however. As trillion-dollar tech giants borrow hundreds of billions of dollars to build out AI data centers and chips, any increase to interest rates could quickly raise their massive costs.
It could also hurt an already pained U.S. consumer. Mortgage rates continue to hover well above 7%, and a rate hike could push borrowing costs higher for auto loans, credit cards, personal loans and other forms of credit.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_orig: Sale of Stefanik family’s D.C. home deemed ‘unusual,’ city records show
articles.title_zh: Sale of Stefanik family’s D.C. home deemed ‘unusual,’ city records show
articles.content_orig:
Emily Russell Report: Sale of Stefanik's DC townhouse to mystery buyer raises questions
A real estate sale involving North Country Congresswoman Elise Stefanik is raising questions after a mystery buyer paid well over the latest asking price for her family's Washington, DC townhouse.
That townhouse was just six blocks from the US Capitol. She purchased it with her parents and brother back in 2010, paying $1.2 million for the three-bedroom home.
Last September, Stefanik listed the townhouse for sale for $2.195 million. The property sat on the market for months. So in November, the price dropped to $1.99 million.
A few more months passed with no buyer for Stefanik’s townhouse, so in February it was taken off the market.
Then last week, the Washington Post broke the news that the townhouse sold in June for $2.9 million, $910,000 more than the latest asking price.
The Post reached out to Stefanik’s office for comment. Her office provided a list of other recent home sales in the area, but according to the Post, nearly all of the examples had more bedrooms and more living space than Stefanik’s townhouse.
Her office told the Post that the townhouse didn’t sell sooner because of a government shutdown, and was later sold in a “commercially reasonable transaction.”
According to The Washington Post, the buyer of Stefanik’s townhouse was a Delaware LLC known as AFS Real Estate Holdings. The Post couldn’t find any online presence or public records about the company.
After her DC property sold for $2.9 million, a real estate company that Stefanik is tied to bought a new home in the DC suburbs in Virginia for $3.3 million.
Stefanik signed a mortgage for that property that’s essentially the difference between what her townhouse sold for and what the new home cost.

articles.title_orig: The $2 trillion chip rally is getting wiped out — here's what history says comes next
articles.title_zh: The $2 trillion chip rally is getting wiped out — here's what history says comes next
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
The biggest one-day rescue in stock market history is coming undone. Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia, and Wall Street's AI doubts are back with a vengeance.
Monday was supposed to be the start of the comeback. Nvidia's ( NVDA ) board brought Huang back at the White House's urging a week after chip stocks' worst week since 2001 , and the group added about $2 trillion in a day , a record $950 billion of it from Nvidia alone.
The sell-off since has hit the whole sector. The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) sank nearly 8% Tuesday, with Micron ( MU ), AMD ( AMD ), and Intel ( INTC ) down roughly 8% to 11% and Broadcom ( AVGO ) and Taiwan Semiconductor ( TSM ) off about 4%. On Wednesday, the index briefly dropped below last Friday's low, as Nvidia and Micron fell as much as 9% and 13%, before buyers stepped in.
The pain spread Wednesday morning, when the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) fell more than 3% and the Nasdaq 100 ( ^NDX ) nearly 5%, with Alphabet ( GOOGL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Amazon ( AMZN ) all lower. By the afternoon, dip buyers had nearly erased the S&P 500's loss.
Huang's return settled the question of who runs Nvidia. It didn't answer whether the debt-fueled AI-building boom will pay off, with tech borrowing costs climbing and the Fed still expected to raise rates on Dec. 9.
Sherwood News' Luke Kawa doesn't blame any single headline. "I think you can pin it on the sum of all the things that everyone's been pointing to for a while," he said on Yahoo Finance's Market Hang Tuesday.
Washington wants to help. President Trump told the New York Post a pardon for Huang is " always an option , I guess, but I don't think it'll be necessary." Asked about a government stake in Nvidia, he said, "It's probably not too late."
"I question what kind of a put it is," GammaRoad Capital Partners chief investment officer Jordan Rizzuto said. "I think it may be a very short-term put." Wednesday's new tariff proposal barely moved futures.
Turnaround Tuesday showed up on schedule. The next part of the script leans bearish. In the 20 times since 1993 that the SPDR S&P 500 ETF ( SPY ) opened a Monday 2% or more higher, it gave back at least half of that gain by Wednesday's close only five times, according to Yahoo Finance calculations. SPY came close to joining them Wednesday morning.
Every one of those fades went on to break the prior Friday's low within three months, most of them within a week. Of the 15 bounces that held up, only a third eventually broke the low in that span. Three of the drops came in the fall of 2008.
For the S&P 500, that low is about 6,883.
A year later, SPY was higher after 17 of those 20 big Monday rallies. In 2018, the Fed hiked into a nearly 20% drop and then paused, and stocks hit a record by April. Alfonso Peccatiello of the Macro Compass likes that echo but still sees more pain first, toward 6,500.
This Fed isn't in a position to blink . Wednesday's PCE report, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, showed core prices up 3.3% from a year earlier, hotter than expected, making a December rate hike all but certain , with more possible early next year.
Read more: How the Fed rate decision affects your bank accounts, loans, credit cards, and investments
Markets close Thursday for Thanksgiving. Advisors Capital Management's Gus Scacco expects Wall Street to wait on Huang's Senate testimony Dec. 3.
"We're going to probably be in purgatory here for a while," he said on Yahoo Finance's Market Hang .

articles.title_orig: ‘If we can solve Riemann, what can’t we do?’: mathematicians shocked and excited by AI breakthroughs
articles.title_zh: ‘If we can solve Riemann, what can’t we do?’: mathematicians shocked and excited by AI breakthroughs
articles.content_orig:
Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain
            the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in
            Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles
            and JavaScript.
Mathematics Álvaro Lozano-Robledo thought the Riemann hypothesis was out of AI’s reach for now. Credit: Bri Diaz/UConn Photo
The news came on a Friday — and it was ground-shaking. For months, reports have mounted of artificial-intelligence models toppling some of the toughest problems in mathematics , plunging the field into turmoil . But the latest claim was the most shocking yet: an AI model had helped to solve the field’s most famous open problem, the Riemann hypothesis .
AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?
AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?
The proof was released on 20 November by mathematician Levent Alpöge at AI giant Anthropic in San Francisco, California, who used an advanced version of the firm’s Claude model. It came in the form of 17 million lines of code in the open-source programming language Lean, which translates mathematical arguments into computer-certifiable code. In a matter of hours, a separate set of mathematicians rushed out a human-written proof of the Riemann hypothesis, which is in the branch of number theory and pertains to the randomness of prime numbers.
Alpöge’s proof has been independently verified by the non-profit organization behind Lean and the Mathlib Initiative, which runs the reference library of formalized mathematics results written in Lean. “We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him,” the community said in a statement on 21 November.
The mathematics community has broadly accepted the claim, although responses differ wildly. Some celebrate Alpöge’s achievement, but others see the development as proof that humans are fighting against machines for the future of mathematics .
Nature hears reactions from four mathematicians on what solving the Riemann hypothesis means to them.
Mathematician Tasmin Chu is part of the Association for Human Mathematics, whose members commit to doing AI-free research. Credit: Elizabeth Xiao
Tasmin Chu , PhD student in mathematics at the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena.
A technology that can autonomously prove the Riemann hypothesis is no trivial matter. I think that it is imperative our society acts to pause AI development as soon as possible. Over the past year, mathematical institutions have faced the impossible task of adapting to the rapidly changing capabilities of AI in real time.
It’s enormously disruptive for early-career researchers — the people who are the intellectual future of our field. Soon other sectors of society will face the same issues.
My reaction is grave concern. AI companies urgently require democratic oversight. I do not think AI’s encroachment into math is inevitable, nor is the death of human mathematical practice inevitable. It’s a choice to disempower ourselves, just as it’s a choice to continue building these technologies despite grave safety concerns. I continue to practice mathematics without LLMs, because I believe it’s critical that scientific inquiry continues in the hands of human beings. Many of us at the Association for Human Mathematics — whose organizing committee I am on — are collectively making the same decision.
Harini Desiraju , postdoc in mathematics at the University of Warwick, UK.
Given the events of the past few months, this news wasn't entirely a surprise, but we need to wait to understand the Lean proof and let the experts verify it. It is several million lines of code, after all.
I am not a number theorist, so I might not have the same emotional attachment to the Riemann hypothesis. Nevertheless, I have deep appreciation for the ubiquity and the importance of the problem in several areas of maths and physics.
As for the recent events, I want to distinguish between formal proofs versus knowledge. It is an impressive feat to solve such a problem. However, because it is a Lean proof over millions of lines, it is going to take a while before the community gets real understanding, and validity of the proof. With an AI-independent approach available as well, it could present a great opportunity for discovery of new ideas and mathematics. We need to see how it all plays out.
There is another discussion to be had, which involves the role of frontier labs in research. Most of us see the potential benefits of this technology, but it is of utmost importance that we work towards a future where the agency is with the scientific community and not a couple of companies.
Mathematician Marcus Du Sautoy is anxious about what’s next for his field. Credit: David Levenson/Getty
Marcus Du Sautoy , m athematician and professor for the public understanding of science at the University of Oxford, UK.
It was real mix of emotions. A part of me says, how exciting to be alive when this great problem was solved! I think even when Fermat’s last theorem was solved, we had the same excitement and the same melancholy: that great motivator is gone.
Mixed in with that, is the complete surprise that it ended up being proved this way. If you’d asked me three months ago, I would never have predicted it.
There’s quite a lot of anxiety about what ‘math 2.0’ is going to look like .
Xin Zhang , assistant professor in mathematics at the University of Hong Kong.

articles.title_orig: China investigates Shanghai Party chief in latest blow to political elite - VOA
articles.title_zh: China investigates Shanghai Party chief in latest blow to political elite - VOA
articles.content_orig:
FILE - Chen Jining, Communist Party Secretary for Shanghai attends a deliberation on the government work report, on the sideline of the National People's Congress at the Beijing Hotel, March 6, 2025. Ng Han Guan/AP hide caption
BANGKOK — Chinese Communist Party authorities are investigating Shanghai party secretary Chen Jining for suspected violations of party discipline, China's anti-corruption watchdog said Tuesday.
The Politburo member is the latest senior official targeted in President Xi Jinping's long-running anti-corruption campaign, which has shown no signs of letting up in scope or depth.
Chen is under investigation by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. The brief announcement by China's Central Commission for Discipline Inspection provided no further details.
A statement released by the Shanghai city government said the Standing Committee of the Shanghai Committee of the CCP "expressed firm support" for the decision to investigate Chen.
The decision sent "a clear and powerful signal that the fight against corruption would continue without pause or retreat," but with "a firm determination to win," the statement said.
The investigation follows sweeping purges under Xi, who has emphasized greater party discipline. The Chinese leader has pursued an anti-corruption campaign for more than a decade, carrying out purges on a scale not seen since Mao Zedong's rule.
"The takedown again shows that Xi Jinping's anti-corruption campaign has no limits," Mingda Qiu, a senior analyst at Eurasia Group, said in an emailed statement. "This is the fourth Politburo member to fall, and the fourth sitting member brought down in the current cycle. The pattern is unprecedented."
The recent Politburo purges highlight how much Chinese politics depend on shifting circumstances, with even officials with qualities that Xi apparently valued being vulnerable to removal, said Joseph Torigian, a professor at American University based in Washington.
"On paper," they appear to be "individuals Xi would appreciate," Torigian said, but afterward, "we could easily come up with hypotheses for why he got rid of them."
Other Politburo members purged include Gen. Zhang Youxia and He Weidong, both senior members of the Central Military Commission, which oversees the armed forces, and Ma Xingrui, a provincial party secretary.
The post of Shanghai party secretary has traditionally been viewed as a stepping stone to China's top leadership. The country's former President Jiang Zemin, its current premier, Li Qiang, and Xi himself previously held the position.
Chen has served as Shanghai party secretary since 2022. He previously held senior positions in Beijing's municipal government and headed the Ministry of Environmental Protection.

articles.title_orig: Almost 2,000 migrants arrive on Spain’s Canary Islands in a single day, breaking a record
articles.title_zh: Almost 2,000 migrants arrive on Spain’s Canary Islands in a single day, breaking a record
articles.content_orig:
Jörg Luyken is a Berlin-based journalist and writer of the German Review , a weekly newsletter on German current affairs
More than 2,000 migrants have reached the Canary Island of El Hierro, marking a new record for arrivals in a single day.
The Spanish coastguard recorded 2,121 migrants arriving aboard 15 boats on the tiny island on Tuesday. A four-day-old baby who was born during the voyage was among them, according to reports.
It is the latest indication that the perilous Atlantic crossing is becoming one of the main routes for illegal migration into Europe .
The figure breaks the previous daily record of 1,580 , set on Nov 14. The island has a population of 12,000 and is the second-smallest of the eight Canary Islands, at roughly 20 miles long and nine miles wide.
Many of the migrants set sail from Senegal in wooden fishing boats on a voyage of more than 800 nautical miles, which can take a week or longer.
Among those arriving on Tuesday was a deceased migrant, as well as about 100 children.
The crossing is among the deadliest of Europe’s irregular migration routes, with more than one in 20 migrants dying or disappearing at sea.
Fernando Clavijo, the Canary Islands’ regional leader, told Spanish radio station Cadena Ser: “Sadly, this is a historic day ... The sailing conditions were favourable and there was a full moon, so these people looking for a better future ended up on our shores.”
Five Spanish coastguard vessels are searching the waters around the islands for migrant boats. Those intercepted on Tuesday were escorted to port by rescue vessels before the occupants were distributed among three temporary reception centres on the islands.
Mr Clavijo warned that El Hierro could not cope with such a large influx. The reception centres are reportedly already overcrowded.
In recent years, arrivals along the West African route have fallen from 47,000 in 2024 to around 18,000 last year.
Although the route remained relatively quiet for much of this year, arrivals have increased in recent weeks. In October, Madrid declared a state of emergency in the Canary Islands, releasing additional funds to expand reception facilities.
The migration crisis is putting pressure on Pedro Sánchez, the Spanish prime minister, before Sunday’s snap election.
In Ceuta , an estimated 10,000 migrants remain on the Spanish territory after tens of thousands surged across the border in July.
The events in Ceuta led to mass demonstrations in several Spanish cities over the government’s handling of the crisis.
Opposition politicians have accused Mr Sánchez of abandoning the people of Ceuta and of attempting to exonerate the Moroccan government for its alleged role in enabling the border crossings.
The prime minister is trailing the conservative Popular Party and hard-Right Vox in the polls, as voters lose faith in his party’s ability to control the situation in the country’s African and Atlantic territories.
During a campaign stop in Tenerife, Santiago Abascal, the Vox leader, described the recent migrant arrivals as an “invasion”.

articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Boehly signs US-backed share swap deal to buy Lukoil global assets
articles.content_orig:
Investors led by U.S. billionaire Todd Boehly's asset management company Eldridge have struck a deal to buy Lukoil's assets outside of Russia, sources confirmed to CNBC.
The U.S. International Development Finance Corporation and Catena Investments, based in the United Arab Emirates, are also parties to the deal, the sources said.
The deal transfers Lukoil's international refineries and other production assets in Bulgaria, Romania, Africa and the Middle East to the U.S.-led group, the sources said. It also includes retail gas stations in the U.S., Europe and Asia, they said.
The U.S. Office of Foreign Assets Control is expected to sign off on the deal but final approval is still needed, the sources said. The deal would give the U.S.-led group about 350,000 barrels per day of production.
The agreement would allow Europe to buy fuel such as diesel previously produced by Lukoil through the U.S.-led group rather than Russia.

articles.title_orig: They graduated college, but they haven’t been able to use their degrees
articles.title_zh: They graduated college, but they haven’t been able to use their degrees
articles.content_orig:
It's getting harder for college graduates to be optimistic about what's next after throwing their graduation caps in the air.
While unemployment among recent college graduates has been cooling as the job market has improved in the past few months, more and more graduates are having to settle for jobs that don't require the years of schooling they've just invested in. Based on data from the job-search platform Indeed, the share of bachelor's degree holders in jobs 12 months after graduation that don't require a college degree, or being underemployed, has risen dramatically in recent years.
Half of the class of 2025 were considered underemployed, above the 2017 to 2019 average of 39%.
Indeed economist Sneha Puri said the surge is due to the low-hire, low-fire job market that has been the story for the past few years. New grads also face a lot of competition for entry-level jobs. Puri said when employers do hire talent, they've been leaning on people "who can hit the ground running, as evident from the growth in job postings being driven by senior-level roles."
"That hits new graduates hardest, because they're most likely to apply for entry-level positions , which not only have seen job postings decline but also get several times as many applications as mid- and senior-level roles, including from people with more experience," Puri said.
Landing a job that doesn't require a college degree can be a short-term solution for new graduates, with long-term consequences.
"For workers who are underemployed or unemployed in their early years after graduating, that can have a stacking effect on their career over time, where they get knocked into a career trajectory that isn't as rewarding, isn't as engaging," Daniel Zhao, chief economist at Glassdoor, told Business Insider.
It could also affect their earning potential, as jobs that don't require degrees often pay less than those that do. For instance, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said there's no formal educational credential required to become a retail salesperson. That job paid an average annual wage of $37,310, per the latest 2025 BLS data, short of the overall average of $69,770. Software developers typically need a bachelor's degree, and Indeed said the average base salary for an entry-level software engineer in the US was about $82,000.
It can be tough to break free from underemployment.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
"Seventy-three percent of graduates who start out underemployed remain so 10 years after completing college , making them at that point about 3.5 times more likely to be underemployed compared with those who start out in a college-level job," a 2024 report from the Burning Glass Institute and Strada Institute said.
Zhao said there's also a risk for employers if they hire a college grad who isn't engaged in their work duties or who would be a better fit in a different position.
It can be easier to find a job in your field depending on your major. The New York Fed found, based on Census Bureau data, that criminal justice, performing arts, and fine arts majors had the top three underemployment rates in 2024. Nursing, aerospace engineering, and civil engineering made up the bottom three.
While computer engineering was among the majors with low underemployment, this major had the second-highest unemployment rate.
Puri expects underemployment to remain elevated for the class of 2026. "An uptick would only reverse once employers again start to recognize the importance of hiring and investing in entry-level talent to train tomorrow's senior level experts," she said.

articles.title_orig: US authorizes SpaceX to deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space
articles.title_zh: US authorizes SpaceX to deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Communications Commission has authorized Elon Musk 's SpaceX to put 1 million artificial intelligence computing satellites in orbit, Chairman Brendan Carr announced on Wednesday.
Carr said in a post on X, the social network owned by SpaceX, that the company's Starmind constellation, and "competitor constellations will use solar power to extend America's lead" in AI.
Musk said in a reply, "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."
The FCC, in its authorization filing , noted that SpaceX's application "received a substantial number of comments from the public, including petitions to deny filed by Kuiper Systems LLC ( Amazon Leo), Viasat Inc. (Viasat), and the American Astronomical Society (AAS)."
In a March petition urging the FCC to deny SpaceX's application, Amazon had labeled the company's Starmind project as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan."
The e-commerce and cloud computing giant is building a competitor to SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, and said it would take SpaceX "centuries" to build the constellation, adding that the company provided scant details about how it would "deliver on these grand claims."
The petition resulted in a rebuke from Carr , who said Amazon "should focus on the fact" that it's falling short of its own satellite deployment milestone.
Representatives from Amazon didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on the FCC's approval.
Other companies have also set their sights on orbital data centers. Google last year announced Project Suncatcher , which it describes as a "moonshot to put AI in space," and launched its first chips into space on a SpaceX rocket and Planet Labs satellite in October.
In March, Jeff Bezos ' Blue Origin petitioned the FCC to let it launch up to 51,600 satellites as part of a low Earth orbit satellite constellation dubbed "Project Sunrise." The constellation would work in tandem with Blue Origin's planned TeraWave satellite internet service, announced in January.
Astrophysicist and author Adam Becker was critical of the FCC move in an email to CNBC on Wednesday.
"Any serious attempt at this is going to further pollute the night sky and runs a serious risk of a cascading chain reaction of space junk collisions, which would be a disaster for all of humanity," he wrote. "Musk and Carr are either profoundly stupid themselves, or hoping the rest of us are too stupid to notice this is nonsense."
SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.
The FCC said in its authorization that it dismissed "comments and concerns raised regarding topics over which the Commission has no authority, including environmental concerns," and concerns about its impact on "optical astronomy."
This story is developing. Please check back for updates.

articles.title_orig: China added nearly 10 times more power capacity than the US in 2025 as the AI race heats up
articles.title_zh: China added nearly 10 times more power capacity than the US in 2025 as the AI race heats up
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING — Jensen Huang ' s return to Nvidia as its CEO underscores how the U.S.-China artificial intelligence race is not only about semiconductors, but tech talent.
"We have to protect our geniuses, and he's clearly a genius," Donald Trump told CNBC about his intervention to bring Huang back. If not, Trump warned, the founder of the AI chip giant could hypothetically have taken a job in China.
The concern reflects how Chinese AI companies have been narrowing the gap with their U.S. counterparts, not just in models, but now in engineering and research talent. China has surpassed the U.S. by share of global AI talent in just three years, according to Carnegie Endowment research.
Nvidia "was shaken without a single chip or model changing," said Winston Ma, an AI investor and adjunct professor of law at New York University. "Whoever builds and keeps that human layer will hold the rest of the stack."
Huang resigned Nov. 12 after reports of an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes has links to Chinese intelligence. He returned on Nov. 23, news which sent Nvidia shares surging.
More than 30 years ago, Huang founded Nvidia as a gaming graphics chip company. The semiconductors gradually became used to mine cryptocurrencies, and now, training cutting-edge AI models.
Huang has more advanced tech coming, Trump told CNBC's Eamon Javers on Monday.
"He's got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about, including me, that nobody else understands," Trump said.
"Jensen could take the next plane to China, and I guarantee you, they would give him whatever he wanted, and then and then they automatically have, you know, all of the things," Trump said. He acknowledged there was "never even a suggestion" that the Nvidia founder was recruited by China.
Trump returned to the U.S. over the weekend from Shenzhen, China, where he met Chinese President Xi Jinping. Earlier in the month, turmoil around Huang's future at Nvidia had gripped global attention.
For Huang's supporters, talent was a critical part of the argument, said Damien Ma, director and Maurice R. Greenberg Director's Chair of Carnegie China.
As the incident has increased scrutiny on the people involved in the U.S.-China tech race, Ma said he's closely watching whether either country restricts AI engineers from leaving. While he expects limited policy changes, other countries such as Singapore and South Korea could benefit from an inflow of AI talent, he added.
Already, many companies are using a mixed-market approach, given engineers in the U.S. make two or three times as much as their Chinese counterparts due in part to foreign exchange rates and AI company valuations.
In the U.S., "you need to have a lot of money to recruit them," said Alex Lu, founder of LSY Consulting — and that can get expensive.
Lu cited the founder of a U.S. consumer research firm, who opted to hire engineers based in China after visiting the country.
It's an anecdote that's frequently repeated by analysts, sometimes with U.S.-trained Chinese staff based in Singapore.
Chinese companies are "very, very aggressive in getting good talent from the U.S. ," said Tidalwave Solutions Partner Rachel Wu, who recruits for large Chinese tech companies and startups.
She also said a Meta engineer in Canada took an offer from a Chinese AI startup for a salary of 1.4 million yuan ($210,000), in addition to stock options.
"There is some truth to Trump's comments given Jensen's knowledge of the AI industry and supply chain," said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst of Omdia. "It would be unwise for the U.S. to let this saga continue to affect its AI ambition, especially when that ambition includes slowing down Chinese progress in AI."
However, Rui Ma, founder of advisory Tech Buzz China, said Huang's background of being a founder makes it more likely that he would have started his own company, rather than taking a managerial role at one.
She also noted Huang's "deep belief in America" and laws that would block him from using his access to TSMC and other suppliers to help a Chinese company.
The U.S. has restricted China's access to advanced Nvidia semiconductors over the last four years. But in early 2025, DeepSeek upended assumptions that chip restrictions could keep Chinese AI capabilities well behind that of the U.S.
A few years ago, only the U.S. and Singapore had the kind of AI talent that Chinese companies were looking for, Wu said. "Today we see the gap has been filled," she said, adding the supply of local talent has increased in the last two to three years.
"The demand is huge," Wu said, saying one ex- Alibaba AI engineering candidate with seven years of experience had more than five offers.
Switching between companies can result in a 25% to 30% pay bump, Wu said. She expects the trend to persist for another two years, although the increase in compensation may not be as high.
Still, restricted access to advanced AI chips plays a role in where the best researchers choose to work.
It's a question of "where I can do my further research and do I have enough resources to do my research," said Lu.
He said industry research suggests "China is becoming a really important pool for talent, while the U.S. is paying 80% of the money."

articles.title_orig: ASML’s CEO makes the case for selling chips to China
articles.title_zh: ASML’s CEO makes the case for selling chips to China
articles.content_orig:

Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer on Tuesday accused Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang of violating federal laws limiting advanced technology exports to China .
In a post on X, Schumer said Huang "shipped extremely advanced chips to China, violating US export control law, in what amounts to the equivalent of selling rocket engines to the Soviets during the Space Race."
Nvidia and the White House did not immediately comment.
Schumer's statement marked an escalation of congressional criticism against Huang, who was reinstated as chief executive of Nvidia on Monday despite claims regarding his relationship with a woman accused of being a Chinese government agent. Lawmakers from both parties are increasingly questioning Nvidia's trade with China, pressing for tighter controls while investigating whether Huang's conduct endangered national security.
Lawmakers have also faulted President Donald Trump for pushing Nvidia to reinstate Huang as CEO.
Schumer and other legislators insist Congress must act rapidly to curtail American chip sales to China. Senator Dave McCormick, a Pennsylvania Republican, said: "Congress must get to the bottom of what happened, and then strengthen our export controls to ensure China can't access our most advanced chips through the back door."
In a separate move on Tuesday, leading Democrats on four House committees wrote to Trump demanding answers about his awareness of Huang’s ties to the suspected agent.
"Your personal relationship with Mr. Huang and your willful blindness to the economic and national security risks posed by this scandal have put the American people at great risk," wrote Representatives Frank Pallone, Gregory Meeks, Jamie Raskin and Robert Garcia, requesting all records of administration contact with the Nvidia board.
"Upon learning that Huang was in a relationship with a suspected agent of the Chinese government, what actions, if any, did Trump take to limit risks to America’s economic and national security?" the lawmakers inquired.
Senator Kevin Cramer, a North Dakota Republican, told CNBC on Tuesday that more protections are needed on exports to China. "We might even have to put a babysitter on Jensen Huang," he stated, adding it would be "just to make sure that he doesn't do something that is going to risk the United States."
Huang will appear on December 3 before the US Senate Banking Committee for a public hearing, panel's chair Tim Scott announced Monday.
Huang is also slated for a private briefing on December 1 with three House panels.
Representative Pat Harrigan, a North Carolina Republican, said Huang's "reinstatement today at this juncture is a mistake." He noted: "We sent a signal that one man’s financial impact on our economy outweighs the importance of good governance, good citizenship, and adherence to the law. That is a dangerous precedent to set."

articles.title_orig: Pakistani astronaut becomes 1st international visitor to China's Tiangong space station (photos)
articles.title_zh: Pakistani astronaut becomes 1st international visitor to China's Tiangong space station (photos)
articles.content_orig:
A Canadian astronaut aboard the International Space Station is celebrating the birth of his third child from hundreds of miles above Earth.
Joshua Kutryk and his wife, Heather Kutryk, welcomed their daughter as the astronaut takes part in a six-month space mission that began in October, the Canadian Space Agency announced on Tuesday.
"Even with the distance between us, we feel incredibly connected as we welcome our new little star into our lives," said the couple in a statement shared by the agency.
Joshua Kutryk, currently on his first space mission, is just the fourth astronaut in history to miss the birth of a child while aboard the International Space Station.
The couple have two older children, aged five and seven.
"We are very proud of our growing family and are looking forward to getting our little crew of five all reunited."
In a statement, the couple said that Joshua's spaceflight was a "childhood dream" come true.
"We hope to show our children that big dreams are worth pursuing, that hard work and determination matter, and that with the support of family and a strong community, extraordinary things are possible," they said.
Prior to becoming an astronaut, Kutryk, from Fort Saskatchewan, Alberta, was a fighter pilot and a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force. He was recruited by the Canadian Space Agency in 2017.
Heather Kutryk said her family had been preparing for years prior to her husband's mission, calling it "a long time coming"
Kutryk was the only Canadian selected to be part of NASA's SpaceX Crew-13 mission, where four astronauts are conducting scientific experiments and testing new technologies in space.
The crew also includes two US astronauts, Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins, and one Russian astronaut, Sergey Teteryatnikov.
Before their take off on 1 October, Heather Kutryk told Canada's public broadcaster CBC News that her family had been preparing for years before the mission, saying it was "a long time coming".
Heather added that her pregnancy was "not exactly planned" but that it was "a great thing".
"I'm not that stressed out. I feel like we have a really good community. I feel well supported by both CSA and Nasa," she said.
"It's six months, I feel like we'll be fine."
In a separate interview with BBC's US news partner CBS News, Joshua Kutryk said he hopes his new child will look at her dad's mission as "making some sacrifice, taking some risk, but doing so in the name of public service and the name, in my case, for Canada."

articles.title_orig: Ladybird's new alpha shows there's life beyond Chromium
articles.title_zh: Ladybird's new alpha shows there's life beyond Chromium
articles.content_orig:
Note: At the time of writing, I was unaware of criticism directed at Ladybird creator Andreas Kling’s public statements. Readers interested in this background can find further context in accounts by Kelson Vibber and Drew DeVault .
After four years of work to build a browser engine from scratch, the Ladybird project released its first downloadable alpha on November 23, offering prebuilt versions for macOS and Linux. Previously, curious users had to compile the browser themselves from its source. Now it’s an installable package with automatic updating.
Ladybird is most notable for what it isn’t: another browser fork. Where Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Opera all run on Google’s Blink engine, and Firefox depends on Gecko, Ladybird’s rendering engine and its LibJS JavaScript engine were written from scratch. “The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork,” project lead Andreas Kling wrote in Monday’s announcement. “The browser around it is modest, but functional.”
Nearly the entire modern web currently runs on three browser engines. There’s WebKit (Safari), Gecko (Firefox), and the biggest of them all, Blink (Chromium). Those limited options mean that web developers often end up optimizing sites for Chromium specifically, since that’s where the majority of traffic is, and as a result, the whole web platform tends to follow suit toward whatever the dominant engine supports.
An independent implementation of web standards has value not just by providing additional competition in the market, but because it can’t help but reveal places where sites depend on Chromium behaviors rather than published specifications. The fact that Ladybird exists isn’t likely to shift the market tides any time soon, but every new browser engine increases the number of implementations that standards can be tested against, which can surface Chromium-specific assumptions and push the ecosystem toward the spec.
The Ladybird project was borne out of Kling’s SerenityOS project, an attempt to develop a new independent OS from scratch, before splitting off as a separate project. Kling formed the Ladybird Browser Initiative, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit funded by sponsorships and donations. The project’s site highlights that there are no sponsored search engine deals supporting the project like many other popular browsers, and sponsoring entities have no say in the project roadmap.
The Ladybird alpha is a rolling release channel that updates automatically, and the downloadable package is a huge step to getting the browser onto the PCs of everyday users. “Ladybird improves quickly, and until now you had to build it from source to see that,” Kling wrote. Though the browser began as C++, in keeping with the ethos of SerenityOS, the project has since started shifting toward Rust , starting with its JavaScript engine.
While it’s exciting to have a new engine option for browsing, the project leader notes that this is still a very early release. The browser build contains a built-in tool for reporting any websites that fail to render or crash the browser. Kling writes, “We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today.”
Microsoft users are still out in the cold on this one for now. The project says that future support for Windows is planned, but it’s macOS and Linux only for now.
I tested the Ladybird alpha version 2026.47.8 on my AceMagic W1 mini PC AMD Ryzen 7 8745HS with 16GB DDR5 and running Fedora Linux 44 with the new KDE Plasma 6.8.3 , and the most surprising thing about the alpha build was how little it feels like alpha software.
The browser seemed to handle most anything I threw at it without issue. Day-to-day tabbed browsing mechanics felt snappy and normal. A 50MB test video file downloaded quickly and smoothly. With a dozen tabs open, switching between them was instant, and the browser felt responsive throughout. Options menus were surprisingly fleshed out for a build this young.
Google Maps loaded instantly, located me, and handled everything I threw at it: adding and removing layers, zooming out from the Midwest, and dropping into Street View in Alberta, Canada in around three seconds. Everything rendered fast enough that my mini PC’s fan spun up noticeably. GitHub’s site, including repository navigation, worked without a hitch. So did YouTube and the news sites I tried.
I could stall the browser, but it took some effort. With about 10 tabs open, I was streaming a 4K test video file from my personal Jellyfin server. Everything worked fine at first, but after skipping around in the file over and over again, the browser eventually got stuck. Mind you, this is an alpha build that I was trying to trip up, not a representation of something inherently broken.
After spending an evening with Ladybird, I can say that while it won’t be replacing Firefox for me anytime soon, I was genuinely impressed that a scratch-made engine could perform this well in such an early state. Most new browser projects are forks of something that already exists. Ladybird is the rare exception, an engine written from nothing, and the alpha runs well enough that if you have a Mac or Linux PC handy, it’s worth downloading a build and poking around yourself. Just remember Kling’s warning: This is nowhere near trustworthy enough to make your daily driver, yet.
What the alpha demonstrates is that a small team of independent developers, funded by donations, has built a browser engine from scratch that handles real web browsing without a fuss. That it works this well this soon, using no existing engine code, is an achievement. I thought I was a Firefox loyalist, but I’ll be keeping an eye on where this one goes.

Technology stocks plunged on Wednesday as excitement over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 's return faded and failed to calm mounting concerns over the sustainability of the artificial intelligence trade.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped nearly 4%. Semiconductor stocks dragged on the index, and the VanEck Semiconductor ETF that tracks the sector plummeted 7%.
After notching one of its best days on record Monday, Nvidia has fallen in the days since and slumped 8% Wednesday. Advanced Micro Devices , Micron Technology , Marvell Technology and Intel all dropped more than 9%, with some plunging further.
Huang's return to Nvidia on Monday briefly revived appetite for tech stocks but didn't fully calm investor concerns over the high costs tied to the AI build-out and worries of a potential slowdown.
Other stocks tied to the AI trade also plummeted. Oracle dropped 8% and CoreWeave and Nebius sank more than 10% each.
Wednesday's declines also came as Wall Street digested a hot inflation reading that fueled concerns that higher interest rates could dent demand for growth stocks, including tech.
Amazon , Tesla and Alphabet each declined about 5%. Microsoft lost more than 2% and Meta traded marginally lower.

articles.title_orig: The AI trade is unraveling days after Jensen Huang's comeback sparked a monster rally
articles.title_zh: The AI trade is unraveling days after Jensen Huang's comeback sparked a monster rally
articles.content_orig:
The AI trade was unraveling on Wednesday, just days after a parabolic rally sparked by Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO.
US stocks barreled toward another losing session the day before Thanksgiving, as the global stock rally triggered by Huang's comeback fizzled out. The Nasdaq 100 was down nearly 4% and the S&P 500 fell 3%.
The move attests to how temperamental the AI trade has become, with big events like Huang's return and the Anthropic IPO unable to lift sentiment and restart the bull rally. Chips, neoclouds, and hypserscalers were all down sharply on Wednesday.
Nvidia dropped 9%, and remains down more than 30% from its early October high. Anthropic, however, made a remarkable round-trip move during the session, dropping as much as 10% but turn positive in afternoon trading. Shares of the Claude maker were up back above their IPO price around 1 p.m. ET, trading around $85.
Dell , notably, dropped 8%, despite reporting blockbuster results for the third quarter after the bell on Tuesday.
"Dell just put up one of the best quarters of the AI cycle, and the stock barely moved, yet another sign that the market is 'over' the AI trade," Luke Lango, an independent tech analyst, wrote in a note. "That's the AI transition period in a nutshell: the fundamentals are booming, but the market is pricing in a slowdown that hasn't shown up in the numbers yet."

Here were the most notable moves in the tech sector in the US:
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
Meanwhile, hot inflation data and the prospect of additional tariffs from the Trump administration were adding to the selling pressure.
Analysts had been mulling whether Monday's relief rally was a dead-cat bounce , a short-lived recovery in stocks before the market makes its way to a new low.
A few worries appear to have triggered the latest bout of selling:
Doubts have been swirling around Nvidia's future , given the ongoing investigation into Huang and uncertainty that continues to loom over the firm's future financing deals and business in China .
"Perception is important, and the current perception of Nvidia's board is not the one that the world's leading chip designer should want," David Morrison, a senior market analyst at Trade Nation, said about Huang's reinstatement in a client note.
Huang is scheduled to testify before the US Senate Banking Committee on December 3 about US chip-export controls, amid mounting congressional scrutiny of Nvidia.
Huang's reinstatement has not removed the political uncertainty surrounding AI, Macquarie Group strategists warned.
"That's because with Huang at Nvidia or not, it's safe to say that the politicians are still 'coming after' AI," they wrote.
Investors are growing anxious that the AI boom is starting to crumble . The market has pent-up anxiety about the trajectory of capex spending , and any hint that firms are either spending too little or too much on AI has triggered a wave of panic-selling recently.
"There is a sense of caution on the markets, with investors not quite sure if they should go all-in on tech again, or whether Monday's Nvidia-fuelled tech rally was a one-day affair," Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said in a morning note.
The prospect of additional tariffs is rattling investors . Reports circulated this week that the Trump administration is readying to unveil a new slate of levies on China and other trading partners this week. It also puts the spotlight on inflation and the likelihood that rates will move higher, a headwind for stocks.
"The threat of another wave of tariffs by Donald Trump could cause unease, particularly if they are seen to cause new inflationary pressures," Coatsworth added, referring to news reports that the Trump administration is preparing to impose fresh taxes on imports from China and other trading partners.
Wall Street is eyeing the possibility that selling will continue for the foreseeable future.
JPMorgan analysts said they were flipping from a tactically bullish to a "Tactically Cautious" view on stocks, pointing to uncertainty around Nvidia in particular.
"In hindsight, it seems obvious that we should have been on the sidelines but we, similar to the market, had viewed NVDA and capital markets activity as the necessary support for Tech to form a bottom and thus whiffed on the tactical bullish call," the bank's market intelligence team wrote in a client note. "Now, the uncertainty surrounding NVDA and peers and opacity over 2028 and beyond makes Tech longs highly uncertain in the very near-term."
Fundstrat's Newton said near-term market trends looked "negative." He said he was searching for signs that tech stocks were starting to gain an edge over defensives, which could happen in the next two weeks, due to seasonal patterns in the market.
"Until that leadership starts to roll over, it's difficult to have conviction that risk appetite has returned in a meaningful way," he said.

articles.title_orig: Cutting-edge Nvidia chips not hard to find for sale in China, despite U.S. ban
articles.title_zh: Cutting-edge Nvidia chips not hard to find for sale in China, despite U.S. ban
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang’s return as CEO to Nvidia hasn’t eased the scrutiny the company faces. The chipmaker still needs to address multiple inquiries into allegations that its advanced GPUs were smuggled into China by a customer, the Singapore-based data center operator Megaspeed, in violation of U.S. export rules designed to slow China’s development of frontier AI models.
The central question for investigators is what Nvidia knew about where those chips ended up and whether Huang’s affair with a Megaspeed executive gave the company reason to doubt Megaspeed’s assurances. Huang’s return doesn’t settle that. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche has suggested Nvidia isn’t a target of an investigation, but California’s attorney general and Congress are pressing ahead, and the Securities and Exchange Commission is reportedly investigating, too.
The U.S. government opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 and requested information from Nvidia about its billions of dollars in sales to the company, concerned that some of the chips Megaspeed bought for data center projects in Malaysia were in fact being diverted to China. Singapore also began investigating similar allegations in 2025. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing.
Diversion of this kind would be a fairly routine issue for a company like Nvidia, whose in-demand chips are the targets of smugglers and resellers. When it comes to compliance and liability for export-control violations, Nvidia and other chip sellers need assurances that the end users of their chips are obeying the rules. However, they also cannot ignore other information that might call the reliability of those assurances into question, export-control attorneys told TechCrunch.
And that’s why Jensen Huang’s affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang was such a problem for Nvidia, likely even more so than her alleged role as a source for Chinese intelligence agencies. If Nvidia personnel, from lower-level employees up to the CEO, had reason to believe that statements from Megaspeed weren’t reliable, the attorneys said, that would increase the company’s legal risk.
“Government investigators likely would want to know, notwithstanding whatever formal assurances were exchanged between the parties, what anyone at Nvidia actually knew about the end use and end users of the chips,” Dan Fisher-Owens, an attorney at the firm Berliner Corcoran & Rowe, told TechCrunch last week.
The concern Nvidia’s board faced when it decided to oust Huang is that he knew more about what Megaspeed was doing with Nvidia’s products than was reflected in any of the compliance statements. The Wall Street Journal reported that Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, were part of a network of businesses that funneled chips to a company in Shanghai. Kang also reportedly introduced his wife to Jensen Huang, whom he had known for a decade.
On Monday, the U.S. government added Megaspeed and its affiliates to a list of companies restricted from U.S. trade due to national security concerns. The U.S. also issued new rules last week barring large data centers that purchase U.S. chips from serving customers in China and other nations seen as problematic by the U.S. government. Nvidia, meanwhile, said it would stop selling licensed chips to China and laid out plans to hire its first compliance officer and create a new board committee focused on export controls.
Nvidia’s board said it reinstated Huang on Monday after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that left it confident his return posed no national security risk. President Donald Trump later said he called into the meeting to give them that assurance.
In a news conference Tuesday, Blanche said that Nvidia was “a good corporate citizen” and suggested it is not the target of an investigation, but Blanche declined to answer questions about the government’s investigation into Megaspeed, which the Justice Department said was ongoing as recently as last week.
“When you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don’t know what you’re talking about,” Blanche said.
Other authorities may be more demanding. Nvidia faces investigations by California Attorney General Rob Bonta and, reportedly , the SEC, both tied to its corporate disclosures. While many details of the investigation still aren’t known, short sellers complained about the company’s decision to stop breaking out its exports to Singapore in financial filings after journalists raised concerns about chip diversion.
Members of Congress from both parties say they want answers from Nvidia, with many citing alarm about China and some questioning the White House’s role in Huang’s return. Three committees in the House of Representatives will privately interview Huang and Nvidia’s top lawyer, Tim Teter, next week. Teter reportedly intervened in the Department of Commerce’s investigation of Megaspeed last year.
“We remain committed to getting answers on the mass smuggling of Nvidia products, their diversion for Chinese military purposes, and their key role in advancing our foremost adversary’s AI capabilities,” the Republican chairs of House committees focused on foreign affairs, intelligence, and China said in a joint statement.
Rep. Brian Mast, the chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has also demanded that the Department of Commerce share extensive data regarding its investigation into chip smuggling, including by Megaspeed and its affiliates.
The Senate Banking Committee will also question Huang in a public hearing on December 3.
“Mr. Huang, Nvidia executives, and the company’s board still owe Congress answers about the company’s compliance with U.S. export controls,” Senator Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democratic member on the committee, said in a statement. “The Trump Administration also needs to explain to Congress what ‘input’ was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement.”

articles.title_orig: Libyan army vows retaliation after 2 naval officers die of wounds from Ukrainian drone attack
articles.title_zh: Libyan army vows retaliation after 2 naval officers die of wounds from Ukrainian drone attack
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine has defended sinking a Russian warship at a Libyan port after one of the country's prominent Western-backed officials accused Kyiv of carrying out "terrorist" attacks and declaring "war" on the North African country.
Ukraine has claimed responsibility for sending naval drones slamming into the Merkury , a Russian corvette, while it sat in the northern Libyan port city of Benghazi early on Sunday.
Dramatic footage showed the seaborne drones hitting the side of the vessel, as Ukraine also said it targeted a military helicopter and a Russian cargo ship carrying weapons for Russia's armed forces.
Russia warned of "very painful consequences" for Ukraine, while Kyiv described the attack as an "exemplary Ukrainian operation."
Ukraine says it has the right to attack Russian assets hundreds of miles away from the frontlines in the east of the country in response to Moscow launching its full-scale invasion of its neighbor nearly five years ago.
But although Kyiv has occasionally hit Russian vessels in the Baltic, Caspian and Mediterranean Seas, the country's long reach—extending far beyond its own borders—has raised fears the grinding war could balloon out further and unsettled even Ukraine's staunch allies. Benghazi is more than 1,000 miles from the trenches of southern Ukraine.
Musa Al-Koni, the vice-president of Libya's Presidential Council in Tripoli, said the attack on the Russian warship was "a declaration of war against the Libyan state," and said authorities in the country "hold the Ukrainian side fully responsible for these terrorist acts."
The North African country is still divided following its civil war, split between the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity—backed by the United Nations—and the military-led eastern administration. The presidential council acts as the head of state.
Rival Libyan authorities in the east of the country, which are generally aligned with the Kremlin, said two Libyan naval officers had been killed in the attack.
Al-Koni said he would refer the matter to the U.N. Security Council and the International Court of Justice in The Hague, which act as the U.N.'s judicial arm.
Ukraine's top diplomat, Andrii Sybiha, said Ukraine was "not 'dragging' anyone into the war or 'transferring' the war anywhere," while a Ukrainian foreign ministry spokesperson said the attack on the Merkury was justified under the United Nations' founding charter, which says each state has the right to self-defense after an armed attack.
"Russia systematically uses its military presence and logistical infrastructure outside its own territory, particularly in Africa, to support military operations and build up capabilities that sustain its war," the spokesperson said.
Russia has leaned more heavily on bases in Libya after scaling down its use of Syrian facilities following the fall of the country's former dictator, Kremlin-aligned Bashar al-Assad, in December 2024.
Moscow has deepened its involvement in swathes of Africa in recent years, including by using its Africa Corps—the successor to the now-disbanded Wagner Group of mercenaries that were influential in the early years of the full-scale war in Ukraine.
A small number of Ukrainian special forces soldiers are reported to have been based in at least two Libyan sites to help carry out attacks on Russian vessels in Libya since late 2025.
The guided-missile Merkury , which has only been in service since 2023, was en route back to Russia, according to officials from Libya's eastern government . It was described as stopping in Libya to refuel and bring on board fresh supplies.
Italy's government, which has largely backed Ukraine despite its right-wing leadership, called the operation a "mistake" and said it had violated Libya's sovereignty.
Meanwhile, Zelensky confirmed on Tuesday that Kyiv was behind an attack on a Russian cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday.
The Sparta II was traveling from St Petersburg to Russia's Baltic Sea exclave of Kaliningrad when drones smashed into the vessel, prompting all crew members to be evacuated. The vessel was later towed into Russian waters after drifting, ablaze, into Finland's territorial waters.
Finland shares more than 800 miles of border with Russia and has been a vocal advocate for Ukraine as one of NATO's newest members.
But Finland's prime minister, Petteri Orpo, said war was "spilling over into our immediate vicinity," while the country's defense minister said Helsinki had made it clear to Kyiv there were safety and environmental risks involved in targeting Russian assets near civilian shipping routes.

articles.title_orig: Colombian police storm supermarket to free 20 held hostage for 17 hours
articles.title_zh: Colombian police storm supermarket to free 20 held hostage for 17 hours
articles.content_orig:
Colombian security forces have freed around 76 shoppers and employees who had been held hostage for about 17 hours at a supermarket in the city of Cartagena.
Gunmen had stormed into the building at 08:00 local time (13:00 GMT) on Tuesday after what Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella described as a failed attempt at robbing an armoured car carrying money.
They held those inside at gunpoint while trying to negotiate their getaway.
With the situation becoming ever more intense as the day progressed, de la Espriella gave the green light for special forces and police to launch a daring operation to free the hostages, killing one gunman.
Residents living near the supermarket reported hearing explosions as the security forces moved into the building.
Police later confirmed that officers had used stun grenades to overpower the hostage-takers. Four have been arrested.
De la Espriella described it as "an extraordinary joint operation", which he said had been carried out "flawlessly".
He flew into the northern city to oversee the operation personally. He could be seen flanked by the commanders of the operation with a handgun strapped to his belt, in footage released following its conclusion.
De la Espriella said the gunmen had been given the chance to hand themselves in but had refused.
Earlier in the day, the assailants had freed 10 of the hostages, among them elderly women.
But they continued to hold around 20, even as a police helicopter hovered above and special forces teams prepared to enter the building, located in a popular shopping centre.
Local media report that, as well as asking for safe passage out of the supermarket, the gunmen also demanded nearly $2m (£1.5m) and armoured vehicles.
De la Espriella said they had no political affiliations but had taken the hostages once their plan to rob a cash-laden armoured car had been foiled.
"It's not that a terrorist group carried out a kidnapping - no, these are criminals who were caught off guard, had no way out and then kidnapped a group of people," he said.
Johan Correa, one of the rescued hostages, described to local media how the gunmen, who he said had been disguised, had entered the supermarket, where he worked.
"We had just started our shift when some guys dressed as police officers came in and started robbing the place," he said. "They were robbers, but we thought they were police."
He added that he and other hostages had been locked in a cold storage room, face down with their hands tied.
"We were there for more than four hours, lying on the floor with our hands tied, and it was a really tough experience."
Another employee, Dayro Rafael Velázquez Castrillo, told Caracol radio that the assailants wore masks and had been armed with guns and knives.
Velázquez said the gunmen repeatedly threatened the hostages, telling them that they had rigged the exits with explosives.
He said that "thank God" they had been rescued, describing moments of tension as they heard explosions and a helicopter flying above.
Photos taken during the rescue operation show armed soldiers inside the building as people kneel with their hands behind their heads.
It is unclear from the photos whether those kneeling are hostages or the hostage-takers.
Local media report that the authorities feared that some of the gunmen may have tried to pass themselves off as hostages as the rescue mission unfolded.
The identities of the four arrested have not yet been released.
The hostages are being reunited with their families after being checked over by medical teams, according to the mayor of Cartagena.
Many anxious relatives had spent hours waiting for news outside the perimeter place around the supermarket by security forces.
A woman called Sandra told Caracol that her 76-year-old mother was one of those being held hostage.
Sandra's mother - among a group of elderly people released after six hours - was reunited with her daughters and grandchildren.
Footage recorded by local media showed bystanders cheering as some of those freed were escorted to ambulances waiting nearby.
But with around 20 people still inside the building, tension outside rose and police said they had to stop some of the relatives from breaching the perimeter.
At one point, flights into the city were halted, with planes diverted to Barranquilla.
Special forces, including units specialised in dealing with kidnappings, were deployed to Cartagena, a popular destination among foreign and Colombian tourists.
Cartagena's Mayor Dumek Turbay called for calm but the granddaughter of one of the hostages told Colombian newspaper El Tiempo that "this shows we're not safe anywhere".
De la Espriella was elected earlier this year on a promise to crack down on Colombia's criminal groups.
He had travelled to the central city of Villavicencio to inspect the damage caused by a car bomb that detonated outside the regional government's offices on Tuesday.
While de la Espriella blamed the leader of a dissident rebel group for that attack, he was adamant that the hostage takers were "simple bandits" without political affiliations.
